overview: Serko is an Auckland (Parnell, NZ) headquartered corporate travel technology company that builds booking and travel-management software used by travel management companies (TMCs), corporates and SME travellers. It monetises through three product lines: Booking.com for Business (Serko powers the SME business-travel layer of Booking.com under a revenue-share arrangement, the single largest revenue source), Zeno (its own online booking tool, market leader in Australasian managed travel and a mid-market player in the US), and GetThere (a legacy enterprise corporate booking tool acquired from Sabre on 7 January 2025). FY2026 (year to 31 March 2026) delivered total income of NZ$120.9m (+34%) and positive EBITDAFI of NZ$6.5m, but a net loss after tax of NZ$17.7m, negative free cash flow of NZ$4.4m, and accumulated losses of NZ$177.5m — Serko has never reported a profit at the net line, and the share price has continued sliding to fresh 52-week lows through September 2026 despite reaffirmed FY2027 guidance, as the market weighs falling take rates and AI-disintermediation risk against a still-growing volume base.

business_model.summary: Serko does not sell software subscriptions in the classic SaaS sense. It earns (a) a share of hotel supplier commissions generated on the Booking.com for Business platform, recognised only once a stay is completed (measured as Completed Room Nights, CRN), and (b) per-transaction booking fees charged to TMCs for bookings processed through the Zeno and GetThere platforms. Revenue is therefore transactional and volume-linked rather than contracted recurring revenue, which means it is directly exposed to business-travel volumes, hotel room rates and — critically — to a contractual commission rate that steps DOWN as volume grows. FY2026 revenue was NZ$119.4m plus NZ$1.5m of other income (mostly R&D tax incentive) for NZ$120.9m of total income.

revenue_streams.name: Supplier commissions revenue (predominantly Booking.com for Business)
revenue_streams.trend: volume growing fast, unit rate declining
revenue_streams.description: NZ$73.4m of FY2026 revenue (+35% YoY). Serko takes a share of hotel supplier commissions on bookings made through Booking.com for Business, recognised on completed stays. FY2026 Completed Room Nights 4.3m (+31%); active customers 301k (+36%). But average revenue per CRN (ARPCRN) FELL 4% to EUR9.25 in FY2026 and fell a further 11% to EUR8.70 in Q1 FY2027, as both hotel room rates softened and the contractual commission tier stepped down (blended rate 48.7% in FY2026 vs 50% prior). This revenue line is also reported net of NZ$6.1m (FY2025: NZ$3.6m) of jointly-agreed marketing fees paid back to the customer.

revenue_streams.name: Travel platform booking revenue (Zeno + GetThere)
revenue_streams.trend: grew on acquisition, organic growth flat to declining
revenue_streams.description: NZ$39.1m of FY2026 revenue (+43% YoY), but the increase is almost entirely the first full year of GetThere (NZ$16.1m). Underlying Australasian Zeno volumes grew only 1.3% in FY2026 (4.1m online bookings) — management itself describes Australasia as 'a mature, reliable business'. Per-booking fees are charged to TMCs, recognised at time of booking.

revenue_streams.name: Expense platform revenue
revenue_streams.description: NZ$4.2m in FY2026, down from NZ$5.3m. Serko sold the InterplX US expense business to Cerebri AI on 30 September 2025 for a royalty on future revenues, booking a NZ$2.0m non-cash loss on disposal; it now partners with third-party US expense providers rather than owning a standalone product.

revenue_streams.name: Services and other revenue
revenue_streams.description: NZ$2.7m combined (installation and chargeable work orders plus other). Serko discloses that supplier commissions and travel platform booking revenue together made up 94% of total revenue in FY2026.

business_model.customer_type: B2B and B2B2C. Serko rarely holds the end-corporate relationship directly: Booking.com for Business revenue flows through a single commercial partner (Booking Holdings), and Zeno/GetThere are distributed via TMCs such as Flight Centre Travel Group and American Express Global Business Travel who own the enterprise client relationship and service layer. The 301k-325k 'active customers' cited by Serko are Booking.com for Business SME accounts, not Serko's own contracted customers.
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2026 revenue by customer location: Europe and Other NZ$75.1m (63%, this is predominantly the Booking.com for Business contracting entity in the Netherlands rather than genuine European end-demand), Australia NZ$25.6m (21%), US NZ$16.0m (13%), New Zealand NZ$2.6m (2%). The Europe line materially overstates European end-market exposure and understates the true geographic spread of the underlying travellers — Serko explicitly notes revenue is attributed by customer location, 'which may differ from the location of the traveller'.
business_model.customer_concentration: SEVERE and disclosed. Two customers accounted for NZ$84.9m of FY2026 revenue — 71% of total revenue (FY2025: NZ$65.4m, 74%). One single customer represented NZ$11.7m of trade receivables/contract assets at 31 March 2026. Booking.com is overwhelmingly the larger of the two.
business_model.unit_economics: Booking.com for Business: FY2026 average commission per CRN (AComPCRN, i.e. the gross supplier commission pool) was around EUR19.3, of which Serko retained roughly EUR9.25 (ARPCRN) — a blended share of about 48.7%, down from 50%. Zeno/GetThere: FY2026 average revenue per booking (ARPB) fell to roughly NZ$12 group-wide (from NZ$12.85 in FY2025) as the lower-priced GetThere mix diluted the average; Australasian ARPB was around NZ$5.58 and declining ~2%. Note the group ARPB and Australasian ARPB are on different definitions and should not be compared directly.

main_competitors: Navan (formerly TripActions, Nasdaq: NAVN since Oct-2025)
American Express Global Business Travel / Egencia
Sabre (also Serko's GetThere counterparty and a supplier)
competitive_position.market_position: Clear leader in the small Australasian managed-travel OBT market, where Zeno is entrenched with the dominant local TMCs. In the US, Serko describes GetThere as 'the second largest independent corporate booking tool in the US market' — but this is explicitly footnoted in the FY2026 annual report as 'by volume, based on management estimate', is not independently verified, and refers to a declining legacy product. Globally Serko is a small player: NZ$121m of revenue against SAP Concur (part of a ~USD$30bn+ revenue software company) and Navan (~USD$613m revenue for the 12 months to July 2025, +32%). Serko's largest business, Booking.com for Business, is a white-label engine inside somebody else's brand — Serko has scale in transactions but not in brand or in owning the customer. Rivals are also moving fast on AI: SAP Concur has begun rolling out AI booking, receipt-analysis and meeting-location agents inside Joule, and Navan has deployed an AI 'room intelligence mapper' to normalise hotel content across GDS and OTA sources including Booking.com — both direct moves onto ground Serko is trying to claim with Serko.ai.
competitive_position.market_share: Not reliably quantifiable from disclosure. Serko is a leader in Australasia (a market of roughly 4.1m online bookings a year for Serko), a distant challenger in the US, and its Booking.com-derived volume (4.3m CRNs in FY2026, 1.4m in Q1 FY2027 alone) is a rounding error against Booking Holdings' total room nights. The GBTA sizes the global business travel market at ~USD$1.71trn of spend in 2026, against which Serko's ~NZ$121m of revenue implies a vanishingly small share — which cuts both ways (long runway, but also no evidence of share capture outside the Booking.com channel).

moat_factors.factor: Booking.com partnership (contractual position, not a moat)
moat_factors.description: This is the biggest single source of revenue and is frequently described as a moat, but the contract terms argue the opposite. The five-year renewal runs 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2029; either party can terminate for convenience on 12 months' notice; the arrangement is NON-EXCLUSIVE, allowing Booking.com to redirect traffic to competing platforms under agreed conditions (Serko is currently the sole platform provider by choice, not by right); and the revenue share steps DOWN with volume — 50% below 4.3m CRNs, roughly 40% blended at 6m CRNs, roughly 32% blended at 8.6m CRNs. Serko reached 4.3m CRNs in FY2026, so it has now exited the top tier permanently. Growth in this channel structurally lowers Serko's take rate from here. Booking Holdings also holds extended preferential investor rights. This is a distribution dependency, not a moat.

Zeno is deeply embedded in the workflows of the dominant ANZ travel management companies (Flight Centre, Amex GBT). Replacing an OBT inside a TMC's service stack is disruptive and slow, which is why Australasian revenue has been stable for several years. But this is also the source of the weakness: it is a small, mature market growing at 1-2% in bookings, and stability is not growth.

Serko's own stated AI advantage — decades of corporate travel behaviour data across millions of bookings a year, plus supplier connectivity — is genuinely differentiated versus a generic LLM wrapper, and is the explicit foundation of the Serko.ai thesis. It remains commercially unproven: Serko.ai was still in closed/expanded beta through Q1 FY2027 (quarter to 30 June 2026), with open beta targeted for Q3 FY2027 (quarter to 31 December 2026). No revenue has yet been attributed to it, and competitors (SAP Concur's Joule agents, Navan's AI content tooling) are shipping comparable AI features in parallel.

moat_factors.factor: Supply and content connectivity (NDC, GDS, aggregation)
moat_factors.description: Serko has built direct NDC connections (Qantas NDC activated July 2025), Sabre hotel aggregation, and an Amadeus NDC rollout. Content breadth is a real barrier for a subscale entrant, but Amadeus, Sabre, Concur and Navan all have the same or better connectivity, so it is table stakes rather than an advantage.
Serko is largely invisible to the end user. The SME channel carries the Booking.com brand; the enterprise channel carries the TMC's brand. Serko captures none of the brand equity it creates.

weaknesses: 71% of FY2026 revenue came from just two customers, with Booking.com the dominant one — the most acute concentration risk of any comparable NZX-listed technology company

The Booking.com commission rate declines as volume grows (50% below 4.3m CRNs, ~40% at 6m, ~32% at 8.6m). Serko crossed the 4.3m threshold in FY2026, so the FY2030 aspiration of NZ$250m of revenue implicitly requires volume growth to outrun a steadily falling take rate

ARPCRN is falling faster than expected: -4% to EUR9.25 in FY2026, then -11% to EUR8.70 in Q1 FY2027 (lower hotel room rates plus tiering). Volume growth of 39% in Q1 FY2027 translated into far less revenue growth

GetThere is a declining legacy asset. Management stated on the FY2026 call that GetThere revenue is expected to DECLINE modestly in FY2027 after contributing NZ$16.1m in FY2026; H1 FY2026 disclosure noted 'expected customer exits' were merely occurring more slowly than assumed, and that 'new sales [were] below target'. The migration of GetThere customers onto Zeno/Serko.ai remains the unproven part of the acquisition case
The Australasian core — the only business Serko genuinely controls end to end — grew online bookings just 1.3% in FY2026 with ARPB declining ~2%

No profitability track record: accumulated losses of NZ$177.5m at 31 March 2026, NZ$138.7m of unrecognised NZ tax losses, and a deferred tax asset that the company itself declines to recognise because 'it is not currently considered probable that future taxable profits will be available'
Serko does not own the customer relationship in either of its two largest channels, which limits pricing power and makes it substitutable at the platform layer

The share price has continued to make fresh 52-week lows through September 2026 (down to roughly NZ$1.13-1.33 depending on source/date, versus NZ$1.27 low disclosed as at late August) even after Q1 FY2027 guidance was reaffirmed, suggesting the market's concern is structural (take-rate compression, AI disintermediation) rather than a single data point that could be resolved by one good quarter

growth_drivers: Booking.com for Business volume scaling — Completed Room Nights up 31% to 4.3m in FY2026 and up 39% to 1.4m in Q1 FY2027; active customers 301k at FY2026 and 325k at Q1 FY2027. This is genuinely compounding, though revenue growth lags volume growth because of tiering

Serko.ai, the multi-agent AI booking/expense agent — closed beta launched May 2026, expanded to several hundred more users in Q1 FY2027, open beta targeted Q3 FY2027, and intended to become the foundation of all Serko managed-travel products. This is the central bet of the Serko 2030 strategy but is pre-revenue

The defined US corporate segments initiative — targeting US corporates that move large groups regularly (management sizes the initial target industries at USD$16-24bn of annual accommodation spend, on its own estimate) via Booking.com for Business rather than a full enterprise programme. Two organisations signed as of Q1 FY2027; management guided this initiative to contribute NZ$2-6m of FY2027 revenue and says it is still 'testing and refining' before scaling — the width of that contribution range is the primary driver of the NZ$6m spread in FY2027 total income guidance

GetThere as a US beachhead — it provided instant US operational presence, enterprise customer relationships and transaction data that management says 'would have taken years to build'; the growth case rests on migrating that installed base to Serko.ai/Zeno rather than on GetThere's own revenue, which is expected to decline
NDC and content modernisation (Qantas NDC live July 2025, Sabre hotel aggregation, Amadeus NDC) allowing Serko to offer richer content and defend Australasian share

Secular business-travel spend growth — GBTA forecasts global business travel spend rising ~7.2% to a record USD$1.71trn in 2026, though trip VOLUME (which is what Serko is actually paid on) is forecast to grow only ~1.3%, with the spend growth coming from higher prices

business.risk: Booking.com partner concentration and contract expiry
business.description: Booking.com is the largest of two customers that together were 71% of FY2026 revenue. The current agreement runs only to 31 March 2029 and either party may terminate for convenience on 12 months' notice — meaning Booking.com could in principle serve notice at any point from around March 2028 (or earlier, with effect after the term). The arrangement is non-exclusive, so Booking.com is contractually free to route traffic to competing platforms. Booking Holdings has the scale, capital and engineering capability to in-source the business-travel layer, and hired-away talent flows both ways (Serko's COO Matthew Gerrie spent a decade at Booking Holdings). Loss or material renegotiation of this contract would be existential rather than merely damaging. No public disclosure of renewal discussions for the post-2029 period has been found as at September 2026.

Not a risk of something going wrong — a contractual certainty already in effect. Serko's blended Booking.com commission rate fell from 50% to 48.7% in FY2026 and falls further toward ~40% at 6m CRNs and ~32% at 8.6m CRNs. Every unit of volume growth dilutes the take rate. Management's counterargument (marginal cost is near zero so incremental contribution is still positive) is fair on gross margin but does not rescue the revenue line: Q1 FY2027 showed 39% CRN growth alongside an 11% ARPCRN decline.

GetThere is a legacy enterprise booking tool whose customers were, at acquisition, expected to exit over time. FY2026 contribution was NZ$16.1m; management guided FY2027 GetThere revenue to decline. If migration of that base onto Zeno/Serko.ai does not convert, the NZ$17.3m of FY2025 business-combination cash outflow bought a melting ice cube plus optionality. Serko has not publicly disclosed a customer-migration count or a revenue-retention rate against what was underwritten at acquisition — a significant transparency gap.

business.risk: AI disintermediation of the booking UI layer
business.description: This cuts both ways and is the central strategic uncertainty. Agentic AI could let a corporate, a TMC, an airline, or Booking.com itself sit an assistant directly on top of supplier content, bypassing Serko's booking interface entirely — Serko's product is precisely the UI/workflow layer that agents are best at replacing. Serko's counter is that trust, proprietary behavioural data, policy enforcement and supplier connectivity are the hard parts, not the chat interface. Trade press coverage in September 2026 illustrates the mechanism in a live competitor product: Navan has deployed an 'AI room intelligence mapper' that normalises and re-ranks hotel content pulled from GDS, Booking.com and other OTA sources before a traveller ever sees it — an AI layer sitting exactly where Serko's own value proposition lives — while SAP Concur is simultaneously rolling out AI booking and expense agents inside Joule. Independent commentary on the FY2026 result attributed Serko's six-year-low share price largely to a sector-wide de-rating of SaaS incumbents on exactly this fear, and the stock has fallen further to new 52-week lows since, rather than stabilising.

Navan listed on Nasdaq in October 2025 at a USD$6.2bn valuation with ~USD$613m of revenue growing 32%, and SAP Concur remains the dominant incumbent with enterprise distribution Serko cannot match. Amadeus Cytric, Amex GBT/Egencia, TravelPerk and Spotnana all compete for the same mid-market and enterprise seats. Serko's sub-NZ$165m market capitalisation gives it far less capacity to fund an AI arms race.

Online bookings +1.3% and ARPB -2% in FY2026. The most defensible part of the business is not a growth engine, so essentially all growth must come from the two least-controlled channels (Booking.com) or the least-proven ones (US corporates, Serko.ai).

financial.risk: Persistent losses and no recognised path to statutory profit
financial.description: Net loss after tax of NZ$17.7m in FY2026 (FY2025: NZ$22.0m), and losses in every year of the recent record. Accumulated losses NZ$177.5m. Unrecognised NZ tax losses NZ$138.7m, with the company stating it is not probable future taxable profits will arise to use them. On the FY2026 call management flagged FY2029-FY2030 as the potential profitability inflection point, contingent on platform modernisation delivering cost rationalisation — a three-to-four year wait with execution risk throughout. The FY2027 total spend guidance (NZ$132-140m) exceeds total income guidance (NZ$128-134m) at every point of the range, so a statutory loss in FY2027 is guided, not merely likely. Sell-side consensus as of September 2026 has pushed the first forecast annual profit out to CY2028.

financial.risk: Cash burn against a finite, non-replenished balance sheet
financial.description: Cash and short-term deposits were NZ$54.1m at 31 March 2026 (NZ$14.1m cash at bank plus NZ$40.0m term deposits), down NZ$7.3m over the year, and down from NZ$61.4m at March 2025 and NZ$82.0m at September 2024. Free cash flow was negative NZ$4.4m in FY2026 (worse than negative NZ$1.9m in FY2025). The company states average monthly cash burn of NZ$0.5m including the one-off GetThere outflow. There is NO debt, which is a genuine strength, and cash covers several years of burn at current rates — but management's own FY2027 expectation implies continued cash burn, so the balance is still shrinking, not compounding. NOTE: the widely circulated figure of 'NZ$14-16m of cash' refers only to the cash-at-bank line and understates liquidity by NZ$40m of term deposits.

financial.risk: Guidance ambiguity on FY2027 free cash flow
financial.description: Reporting from the FY2026 call is contradictory: the CFO is quoted as expecting 'positive free cash flow' at the guidance midpoint while other commentary cites an expected cash burn — and the FY2026 annual report itself gives no explicit FY2027 free cash flow guidance, only total income and total spend ranges. Investors should treat 'FY2027 cash-flow breakeven' as an unconfirmed management aspiration, not a stated target.

The majority of costs are in NZD while the largest revenue stream (Booking.com) is invoiced in EUR. FY2026 saw NZ$3.8m of forward exchange contract losses and NZ$0.5m of net FX losses as EUR strengthened — together roughly 60% of the EBITDAFI result, and a meaningful reason the statutory loss did not narrow further. For FY2027 Serko has designated EUR32.0m of forwards as accounting hedges at an effective rate around 1.9766, which will reduce P&L volatility but also fixes the rate. A NZ$1.1m negative cashflow hedge reserve sits in equity at 31 March 2026.

Share-based payment expense of NZ$7.246m in FY2026 (up from NZ$5.429m), against EBITDAFI of NZ$6.5m — i.e. the non-cash equity comp added back to reach positive EBITDAFI exceeds EBITDAFI itself. A further 2,146,013 RSUs were issued 22 September 2026 at a grant price of NZ$1.5720 (the 20-day VWAP to 4 June 2026), taking outstanding RSUs to 8,712,795 against 126,139,278 ordinary shares on issue — RSUs now equal roughly 6.9% of shares on issue, up materially from the ~5,091,165 RSUs (~4%) disclosed at 31 March 2026. With the share price having fallen further, to roughly NZ$1.13-1.33 through September 2026 (versus grant prices historically around NZ$3.02 and even the latest NZ$1.572 grant), retention economics remain strained and dilution continues to run ahead of the FY2026 disclosed level.

financial.risk: EBITDAFI is a heavily adjusted measure
financial.description: Serko's headline 'profit' metric excludes interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation, FX gains/losses, forward contract gains/losses, fair value movements and impairments. To get from a NZ$17.7m net loss to NZ$6.5m of EBITDAFI requires adding back NZ$18.0m of D&A, NZ$2.1m of impairments/disposals, NZ$3.8m of FEC losses and NZ$0.5m of FX. It is not audited, is not comparable across companies, and — because Serko capitalises development costs (NZ$8.6m in FY2026) which then amortise — it flatters the economics of a business that spends heavily on software build.

regulatory.risk: Travel data privacy and cross-border data rules
regulatory.description: Serko handles traveller PII across NZ, Australia, the EU (GDPR), the US, India and China, with R&D operations in Foshan, China and India. Any tightening of cross-border transfer rules or a data breach in a trust-dependent business would be damaging. Serko has not disclosed any current regulatory action or breach.

regulatory.risk: Airline/hotel distribution regulation and NDC transition
regulatory.description: The industry shift from GDS-based distribution to airline-direct NDC changes who controls content and economics. Serko is investing to stay connected (Qantas NDC, Amadeus, Sabre), but NDC also enables suppliers to disintermediate aggregation layers. Not a compliance risk so much as a structural distribution risk with a regulatory overlay.
NZ$1.1m of the NZ$1.5m of FY2026 other income was the NZ R&D Tax Incentive. Small in absolute terms but it is roughly 17% of reported EBITDAFI, and policy change would remove it.

regulatory.risk: Antitrust / platform regulation affecting Booking Holdings
regulatory.description: Booking Holdings faces ongoing scrutiny in the EU (Digital Markets Act gatekeeper designation) and elsewhere. Any regulatory pressure that changes how Booking.com structures partner arrangements or commission flows could indirectly affect Serko's largest revenue stream. No evidence found of a current action specifically affecting the Booking.com for Business/Serko arrangement.

macro.description: Serko is paid per booking and per completed room night, so revenue tracks travel VOLUME, not travel spend. GBTA forecasts 2026 global business travel spend +7.2% but trip volume only +1.3% — the growth is coming from higher prices, which does not help Serko's transaction-fee lines and only partly helps commissions. A corporate cost-cutting cycle, a recession, or a shift to video meetings hits the top line directly and quickly.

Because Serko earns a share of a percentage commission on hotel spend, falling room rates cut revenue per room night even at flat volume. Management explicitly attributed part of the ARPCRN decline (to EUR8.70 in Q1 FY2027) to lower room rates. This is outside Serko's control and compounds the tiering effect.

Serko's FY2027 guidance is explicitly caveated on 'the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on business travel demand'. In the Q1 FY2027 update the company said Middle East bookings were under 3% of group CRNs pre-conflict and the identifiable impact was a low single-digit (1-2%) headwind — but the caveat remains in guidance, and broader geopolitical shocks (as in 2020) have historically been devastating for this business.

Serko has no debt, so rising rates do not hurt it directly. The exposure runs the other way: falling rates reduce interest income on the NZ$54.1m cash/deposit balance. Finance income fell from NZ$3.5m to NZ$1.5m in FY2026 — a NZ$1.9m headwind to the pre-tax result, equivalent to roughly 30% of EBITDAFI. Lower NZ rates continue this drag. Indirectly, a higher discount-rate environment is punishing for long-duration, loss-making small caps — analysts explicitly cited a higher discount rate as a factor in cutting Serko's target price alongside more moderate revenue growth assumptions.

macro.risk: Currency translation on a NZD reporting base
macro.description: Revenue predominantly EUR/USD/AUD, costs predominantly NZD. A strengthening NZD compresses reported revenue; a strengthening EUR generates hedge losses in the P&L (as in FY2026). Either direction can hurt depending on which side is hedged.

execution.risk: Serko.ai must be delivered and commercialised
execution.description: The entire Serko 2030 case (NZ$250m revenue, NZ$100m free cash flow by FY2030) rests on an AI product that was still in expanded beta through Q1 FY2027, with open beta only targeted for Q3 FY2027 and no disclosed commercial model or pricing. There is no revenue attributable to it yet. Management has said Serko.ai will 'eventually form the foundation of all our global managed travel product offerings' — meaning a failed or delayed launch is not a missed opportunity but a failed replatforming. Rival AI features (SAP Concur's Joule agents, Navan's AI content tooling) are already live commercially, raising the bar Serko.ai must clear at launch.

Two customers signed as of Q1 FY2027, with management still 'testing and refining' before scaling and guiding only NZ$2-6m of FY2027 revenue contribution from the initiative. This is the stated reason for the NZ$6m width of the FY2027 income guidance range. Serko has repeatedly found US enterprise selling hard (H1 FY2026: 'New sales below target' for GetThere).

On 10 June 2026 Serko announced that COO Matthew Gerrie (ex-Booking Holdings, joined early 2025) would take responsibility for day-to-day operational performance across commercial, finance, people, technology and product, with co-founder CEO Darrin Grafton's role refocused on 'long-term industry positioning and external partnerships'. David Holyoke was promoted to Chief Product Officer. No departures were announced. Framed by the company as accelerating execution, but a founder-CEO handing day-to-day operations to a recent hire during a period of sustained share price weakness (which has continued into September 2026) is a governance signal worth watching — and it concentrates operational execution in an executive with roughly 18 months' tenure.

Serko capitalised NZ$8.6m of development costs in FY2026 (up from NZ$5.0m) including NZ$5.4m of employee costs, while amortising NZ$15.7m. Capitalisation is a matter of management judgement, is flagged as a key accounting estimate, and directly boosts the EBITDAFI headline. It also creates future impairment risk: goodwill was fully written off (NZ$5.1m impairment in FY2025 and NZ$1.6m disposed with InterplX in FY2026), leaving NZ$21.4m of intangibles of which NZ$13.6m is capitalised software and NZ$4.0m is work in progress, tested at a 11.7% pre-tax discount rate.

The register remains founder-concentrated: co-founder Bob Shaw held 9,444,678 shares (~7.5%) per a 2026 substantial-holder notice, and CEO Darrin Grafton is also a substantial shareholder. Grafton sold approximately 600,000 shares on-market on 18 July 2026 at around A$2.66, about 5.3% of his direct holding — reported as his only on-market sale in twelve months, following RSU vesting; a further RSU-vesting-driven increase in his direct/indirect holding was disclosed around 5 June 2026 (no cash payment involved). There is no evidence of meaningful insider BUYING at the now-lower September 2026 price levels.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: GBTA forecasts global business travel spend to reach a record USD$1.71trn in 2026 (+7.2%), passing USD$2trn by 2030 — a year later than previously forecast. The important nuance for Serko is that trip volume is forecast to grow only ~1.3% in 2026: the spend growth is price-led. Serko is paid on transactions and room nights, so it participates in volume growth, not price growth, except indirectly via percentage commissions on hotel spend (which are currently being offset by falling room rates). The corporate travel technology segment itself is consolidating and re-rating: Navan listed in October 2025 (USD$6.2bn valuation, shares fell 20% on debut), SAP Concur remains dominant, and the whole category is being repriced for agentic-AI disruption risk — a September 2026 trade-press piece on AI-mediated hotel content selection (covering Navan and Concur, not Serko directly) illustrates the mechanism competitors are already deploying in exactly the layer Serko occupies.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High. Corporate travel is one of the first discretionary line items cut in a downturn and Serko's revenue is transaction-linked with essentially no contracted recurring floor. COVID-19 is visible as a crater in Serko's own long-term revenue chart, and the business took several years to recover prior peak volumes.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct (no debt), mildly negative on the income statement (finance income fell from NZ$3.5m to NZ$1.5m in FY2026 as rates and balances fell), and high indirect via equity market appetite for unprofitable long-duration small caps — analysts explicitly cited a higher discount rate in trimming Serko's target price after the FY2026 result.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High. NZD reporting currency, NZD-heavy cost base, EUR-dominant revenue (Booking.com), plus AUD and USD. FY2026 carried NZ$3.8m of forward contract losses and NZ$0.5m of FX losses. FY2027 has EUR32.0m of designated cash flow hedges at ~1.9766 EUR:NZD.
key_input_costs: Employee remuneration — NZ$76.1m of FY2026 opex, 58% of total operating expenses, 400+ staff across NZ, Australia, China, India, UK and US; the India engineering hub is the stated cost-efficiency lever
Cloud hosting — NZ$9.4m in FY2026, up 36%, and scaling with AI workloads
External software development and computer licences — NZ$5.3m and NZ$3.6m respectively, with external development up 267% as AI build accelerated
Share-based payments — NZ$7.2m non-cash in FY2026 and growing further with the September 2026 RSU issuance
macro_factors.regulatory_environment: Not heavily regulated as a business in its own right — no licence regime, no capital requirements, no disclosed contingent liabilities at 31 March 2026. The relevant regulatory exposures are indirect: data privacy across multiple jurisdictions, airline distribution (NDC) rules, and platform/antitrust scrutiny of its largest partner Booking Holdings. This is a comparatively clean regulatory profile; the risks in this business are commercial and competitive, not regulatory.

recent_developments.event: Share price continued to make fresh lows: quoted around NZ$1.33 on the NZX (Forsyth Barr, 25 September 2026) and roughly AUD$1.22 on the ASX foreign-exempt listing (24 September 2026), both well below the ~NZ$1.27-1.46 range disclosed as at late August 2026 and implying a new 52-week low near NZ$1.13-1.20 depending on source. Market capitalisation has fallen to roughly NZ$150-165m. The decline has occurred with no new price-sensitive company announcement in the period, consistent with continued de-rating on structural concerns (commission-tier step-down, AI disintermediation) rather than a single news event.

Capital Change Notice: Serko issued 2,146,013 unlisted Restricted Share Units under the Long-Term Incentive Scheme, grant price NZ$1.5720 (20-day VWAP to 4 June 2026), no exercise price. Following issuance, ordinary shares on issue were confirmed at 126,139,278 and RSUs outstanding rose to 8,712,795 (both filed via ASX Appendix 3G / NZX Capital Change Notice). This resolves the prior verification note about the post-31-March-2026 share count and shows RSU dilution (~6.9% of shares on issue) continuing to build even as the share price used for new grants has fallen well below historical grant levels.

Industry coverage (eHotelier, 3 September 2026) described how AI systems at rival platforms — specifically Navan's 'AI-powered room intelligence mapper', which normalises and re-ranks hotel content sourced from GDS, Booking.com and other OTAs before a traveller sees it — are increasingly mediating what travellers are shown, with hotels losing visibility into how their content is transformed. Serko was not named in the piece, but the mechanism described sits directly in the booking/content layer Serko occupies and underscores the competitive AI pressure referenced in Serko's own risk disclosures.

Q1 FY2027 trading update (quarter to 30 June 2026): Booking.com for Business Completed Room Nights +39% to 1.4m; active customers +35% to 325,000; average revenue per CRN DOWN 11% to EUR8.70 on lower hotel room rates and commission tiering. Two US corporate-segment organisations signed, with management still testing before scaling and guiding NZ$2-6m of FY2027 revenue from the initiative. Serko.ai beta expanded to several hundred additional users, open beta on track for Q3 FY2027. Middle East conflict impact described as a low single-digit headwind (Middle East bookings under 3% of group CRNs pre-conflict). FY2027 guidance REAFFIRMED at NZ$128-134m total income and NZ$132-140m total spend. Forsyth Barr commented the update 'should ease investor concerns over room-night growth' — but the 39% volume / -11% price split is the clearest single illustration of the tiering problem, and the share price has continued falling since this update rather than stabilising.

Leadership restructure announced: COO Matthew Gerrie (ex-Booking Holdings, joined early 2025) given expanded responsibility for day-to-day operational performance across commercial, finance, people, technology and product; David Holyoke (ex-Airbnb, ex-Travel Leaders, joined 2024, led Serko.ai development) promoted to Chief Product Officer and to the Executive Team; co-founder CEO Darrin Grafton's role refocused on long-term industry positioning and external partnerships. No departures announced.

CEO Darrin Grafton's direct and indirect holdings of Serko ordinary shares increased following vesting of RSUs under the long-term incentive plan (no cash payment involved) — company framed as evidence of equity-based alignment. Grafton subsequently sold approximately 600,000 shares on-market on 18 July 2026 at around A$2.66, about 5.3% of his direct holding, reported as his only on-market sale in the prior twelve months.

FY2026 audited full-year result (year to 31 March 2026): total income NZ$120.9m (+34%, at the top end of narrowed guidance), revenue NZ$119.4m, EBITDAFI NZ$6.5m (+137%), net loss after tax NZ$17.7m (improved NZ$4.2m from NZ$22.0m), free cash flow NEGATIVE NZ$4.4m (a NZ$2.5m deterioration from -NZ$1.9m), cash and short-term deposits NZ$54.1m with no debt. Total spend NZ$122.9m equal to 102% of income. GetThere contributed NZ$16.1m in its first full year. Deloitte issued a clean unmodified audit opinion with a going-concern conclusion supported by the NZ$54.1m cash position. FY2027 guidance issued: total income NZ$128-134m, total spend NZ$132-140m — both implying another guided statutory loss. Analysts cut forecasts; consensus target fell from around NZ$3.69 to NZ$3.22 (roughly 7.9%), citing a higher discount rate, more moderate revenue growth and a lower future P/E multiple; FY2027 expected loss per share widened from NZ$0.03 to NZ$0.041. Despite 34% revenue growth the share price fell to what was then a six-year low, and has fallen further since — commentary attributed this largely to a sector-wide de-rating of SaaS incumbents on agentic-AI disruption fears rather than Serko-specific execution failure.

Serko.ai closed beta launched in the US — a multi-agent, intent-driven AI travel assistant positioned as 'not a chatbot layered on top of a booking tool' but a coordinated execution engine. Open beta targeted for Q3 FY2027. Zero revenue attributed to date.

Investor Day: 'Serko 2030' strategy unveiled with three pillars (launch Serko.ai; scale Booking.com for Business; win defined US corporate segments) and an FY2030 aspiration of NZ$250m of revenue and NZ$100m of free cash flow. These are explicitly framed as aspirations, not guidance. On the FY2026 call an analyst directly challenged whether the NZ$250m target implies unrealistic operating leverage; management pointed to platform modernisation and cost rationalisation, and flagged FY2029-FY2030 as the likely profitability inflection.

H1 FY2026 result (six months to 30 September 2025): total income NZ$61.8m (+45%), EBITDAFI NZ$6.1m (+394%), free cash flow POSITIVE NZ$3.0m, net loss after tax widened to NZ$9.5m (from NZ$5.1m), cash NZ$65.0m. FY2026 total income guidance reaffirmed at NZ$115-123m and total spend guidance CUT to NZ$124-128m from NZ$127-133m. H1 FY2026 was FCF-positive and the full year was FCF-negative NZ$4.4m, implying second-half free cash outflow of roughly NZ$7.4m — the burn accelerated materially in H2.

Sold the InterplX US expense management business to Cerebri AI in exchange for a royalty on future revenues (present value NZ$0.2m), recognising a NZ$2.0m non-cash loss on disposal including NZ$1.6m of goodwill. Serko now partners with third-party US payments/expense providers rather than owning a standalone product — a sensible narrowing of focus, but it also removes an expense-side product at exactly the moment Navan is bundling travel and expense.

Completed the acquisition of GetThere from Sabre, alongside a commercial partnership with Sabre. NZ$17.3m of business-combination cash outflow in FY2025 plus NZ$2.8m in FY2026. Provided instant US scale — but is expected to decline in revenue in FY2027.

The five-year Booking.com partnership renewal that governs Serko's largest revenue stream: term 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2029; tiered revenue share of 50% below 4.3m CRNs per year, approximately 40% blended at 6m CRNs and approximately 32% blended at 8.6m CRNs; MUTUAL termination for convenience on 12 months' notice; NON-EXCLUSIVE. Serko reached 4.3m CRNs in FY2026, so the top tier is now behind it. As at September 2026 no public disclosure has been found regarding renewal terms beyond March 2029.

Management states the NZ$6m width of the range is 'primarily driven by the timing of booking volumes from the strategic initiative targeting defined US corporates' — quantified at NZ$2-6m of contribution — i.e. the range depends on an initiative with two customers signed to date. Guidance is explicitly caveated on economic and geopolitical conditions 'including the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on business travel demand'. Comparing midpoints, income of NZ$131m against spend of NZ$136m implies a guided spend-to-income ratio of about 104%, WORSE than FY2026's 102%. Serko is therefore explicitly guiding to reduced operating leverage in FY2027 as it funds Serko.ai and US expansion — a deliberate reinvestment decision, but it means the FY2026 improvement in operating leverage does not continue in FY2027. A statutory net loss in FY2027 is effectively guided.

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Claudia Batten and CEO Darrin Grafton framed FY2026 as 'a year of execution and acceleration' delivering total income at the top end of narrowed guidance with total spend held at 102% of income. CFO Shane Sampson emphasised that 'growth investment is now substantially funded from operating cash flows rather than shareholder funds' — a fair characterisation given operating cash flow of NZ$7.0m, though free cash flow after NZ$9.9m of capex and capitalised development was still negative NZ$4.4m. At the Q1 FY2027 update (29 July 2026) management reiterated confidence in reaffirmed guidance, highlighted the 39% CRN growth and the two-customer US corporate segment start, and described the Middle East conflict impact as minimal to date. No further formal guidance update, investor day, or trading update has been issued between the Q1 FY2027 update (29 July 2026) and 26 September 2026. Management's stated FY2027 focus remains scaling Booking.com for Business, launching Serko.ai to open beta, and testing the US corporate segment before scaling. The FY2026 annual report's framing that 'shifting industry dynamics are creating tailwinds we have not seen before' looks increasingly at odds with a share price that has continued falling to fresh lows through September 2026 without any negative company-specific news in that window — consistent with a market that remains unconvinced by the Serko 2030 narrative rather than one reacting to a new adverse development.

bull_case: Deeply de-rated with a genuine cash cushion and no debt: at roughly NZ$1.20-1.33 (September 2026) and a market cap of roughly NZ$150-165m, NZ$54.1m of cash and term deposits (as at 31 March 2026) represents a third or more of the market capitalisation, implying an enterprise value only modestly above NZ$100m against NZ$120.9m of FY2026 total income (well under 1x EV/Sales). Analyst consensus target remains around NZ$3.10-3.44, roughly 2.5-3x the current price. Serko has no debt and covers its guided burn for years without raising equity — the funding question is real but not urgent

Booking.com for Business volume is genuinely compounding at scale: Completed Room Nights +31% to 4.3m in FY2026 and +39% to 1.4m in Q1 FY2027, with active customers +35-36% to 325,000. Even with the commission tier stepping down, incremental volume carries near-zero marginal cost, so each additional room night still adds gross contribution. Total contribution can keep growing even as ARPCRN falls

Operating leverage was demonstrated in FY2026: EBITDAFI up 137% to NZ$6.5m on 34% income growth, with total spend held at 102% of income; H1 FY2026 was free-cash-flow positive at NZ$3.0m. The business has shown it is capable of positive cash generation when it chooses to slow investment, which materially reduces the probability of a distressed capital raise

Serko.ai is a credible, differentiated shot at the AI transition rather than a purely defensive one: multi-agent execution built on two decades of proprietary corporate booking behaviour, supplier connectivity, and policy-enforcement logic — the parts of the problem that are hard to synthesise. Open beta is on track for Q3 FY2027. If it lands, Serko converts from a per-transaction OBT into a higher-value travel operating layer with new commercial models, which is exactly the re-rating the market is currently refusing to underwrite

The US corporate segment is a real, sized wedge with a now-quantified near-term contribution (NZ$2-6m in FY2027): management estimates USD$16-24bn of annual accommodation spend in the initial target industries — organisations that move large groups regularly but don't need a full enterprise programme. If this converts even modestly it is a channel with no incumbent lock-in, feeding the Booking.com engine Serko already operates

Clean balance sheet and clean audit: no debt, no contingent liabilities at balance date, goodwill now fully written off (removing future goodwill impairment risk), an unmodified Deloitte opinion, and NZ$138.7m of unrecognised NZ tax losses that would shield years of profit if profitability ever arrives
bear_case: The Booking.com relationship is a contractual cliff dressed as a moat. It underpins the majority of revenue (two customers = 71% of FY2026 revenue), the contract expires 31 March 2029, it is terminable by either party for convenience on 12 months' notice, it is NON-EXCLUSIVE so Booking.com may route traffic elsewhere, and Booking Holdings holds extended preferential investor rights. Serko has no disclosed renewal beyond 2029. Booking Holdings has every capability to in-source a business-travel layer it already brands as its own — and Serko's own COO came from Booking Holdings. There is no realistic scenario in which Serko survives in its current form if this contract is lost or materially repriced

Growth is now actively self-cannibalising on price. The revenue share falls from 50% below 4.3m CRNs toward ~40% at 6m CRNs and ~32% at 8.6m CRNs, and Serko crossed 4.3m in FY2026. The evidence is already visible: 39% CRN growth in Q1 FY2027 delivered an 11% DECLINE in revenue per room night. To hit the NZ$250m FY2030 aspiration Serko must roughly double the volume run-rate while its take rate falls by a third — and FY2027 is guided at just 6-11% revenue growth, so the required acceleration has not begun

There is no credible near-term path to profit, and the market's continued sell-off through September 2026 — to fresh 52-week lows, with no adverse new company disclosure in the window — suggests investors increasingly doubt it ever arrives on the stated timeline. FY2026 net loss NZ$17.7m; accumulated losses NZ$177.5m; free cash flow negative NZ$4.4m and DETERIORATING into year-end (H2 FY2026 alone burned ~NZ$7.4m); FY2027 total spend is guided ABOVE total income at every point, implying a spend-to-income ratio near 104% versus 102% in FY2026 — operating leverage goes backwards. Management now points to FY2029-FY2030 for the profitability inflection. The company itself declines to recognise its deferred tax assets because future taxable profits are 'not currently considered probable' — the most honest statement in the accounts

The two things Serko fully controls are not growing. Australasian online bookings grew 1.3% with ARPB down ~2% in FY2026, and GetThere — a NZ$20m+ cash acquisition — contributed NZ$16.1m in FY2026 but is guided to DECLINE in FY2027, with prior disclosure noting customer exits and 'new sales below target'. Serko has never published a GetThere migration count or revenue-retention rate against acquisition underwriting. All growth therefore depends on a partner-controlled channel with a falling take rate, plus two pre-revenue initiatives

Agentic AI is at least as likely to disintermediate Serko as to be captured by it. Serko's product IS the booking interface and workflow layer — precisely what AI agents replace. September 2026 trade coverage of Navan's AI content-mapping tooling and SAP Concur's Joule booking/expense agents shows rivals already shipping AI at the exact layer Serko is still in beta on. Navan listed in October 2025 at USD$6.2bn with USD$613m of revenue growing 32% and bundles travel with expense — while Serko has just DIVESTED its expense product (InterplX, September 2025). The market has already voted twice now: 34% revenue growth produced a six-year-low share price in May 2026, and the stock has fallen further to fresh lows since, without any new negative company disclosure

Reported profitability rests on soft measures and is flattered, and dilution keeps building. EBITDAFI of NZ$6.5m is arrived at only after adding back NZ$18.0m of D&A (against NZ$8.6m of newly capitalised development costs), NZ$3.8m of FX forward losses and NZ$2.1m of impairments/disposals; NZ$7.2m of FY2026 share-based payments — more than EBITDAFI itself — is a real economic cost to shareholders that EBITDAFI ignores, and a further 2.1m RSUs were issued in September 2026, taking RSUs outstanding to 8.7m (~6.9% of shares on issue). Meanwhile NZ$1.1m of the NZ$1.5m of 'other income' is an R&D tax credit, and interest income halved from NZ$3.5m to NZ$1.5m as the cash pile shrank. Strip the adjustments and the business consumed cash in FY2026

Thin, stale sell-side support and a widening credibility gap. Coverage is small (roughly 4-7 analysts), consensus target sits around NZ$3.10-3.44 against a price that has fallen to roughly NZ$1.20-1.33 — a >130% gap that has WIDENED, not narrowed, through 2026 despite repeated downgrades (FY2027 expected loss widened from NZ$0.03 to NZ$0.041 per share after the FY2026 result, and consensus target itself was cut ~7.9% at the same time). Long-term holders are heavily underwater: Serko raised roughly NZ$200m between 2018 and 2022 at an average around NZ$4.99 per share. There is no disclosed insider buying at these lower levels; the CEO sold shares in July 2026 and new RSU grants in September 2026 continued at a lower reference price than prior years
valuation_context: SKO trades around NZ$1.20-1.33 (late September 2026, sources vary by date/exchange) for a market capitalisation of roughly NZ$150-165m, a further decline from NZ$1.465 (~NZ$184m) as at 28 August 2026 and a fresh 52-week low, down well over 50% over twelve months to levels last seen many years ago — despite reporting 34% FY2026 revenue growth and reaffirmed FY2027 guidance at the Q1 FY2027 update. Net of NZ$54.1m of cash and short-term deposits (as at 31 March 2026) and with no debt, enterprise value is now only modestly above NZ$100m against NZ$120.9m of FY2026 total income, comfortably under 1x EV/Sales — a distressed-growth multiple for a company still growing revenue at a guided 6-11% in FY2027. Conventional earnings multiples remain unusable: Serko is loss-making at the net line (FY2026 EPS -NZ$0.14) and guided to remain so in FY2027, with management pointing to FY2029-FY2030 for the profitability inflection (though some sell-side models now show a maiden profit as early as CY2028). Net tangible assets per share were 53.92 cents at 31 March 2026, so the stock now trades close to, or only modestly above, NTA and roughly 1.7-1.9x total book equity of NZ$88.7m — both multiples having compressed meaningfully since August. Analyst consensus remains 'Buy' with an average target of roughly NZ$3.10-3.44 (range approximately NZ$2.48-NZ$4.10) — but coverage is thin (4-7 analysts) and the widening gap between price and target (now over 130%) through September 2026, absent any new adverse company-specific disclosure, reads as the market progressively discounting the Serko 2030 aspiration (NZ$250m revenue, NZ$100m free cash flow by FY2030) rather than a one-off dislocation. The genuine debate is binary and structural rather than a matter of multiple: does the Booking.com for Business channel survive its March 2029 contract expiry and its declining commission tiers, and does Serko.ai convert Serko from a per-transaction booking layer into something an AI agent cannot route around, before rivals' own AI tooling (Navan, SAP Concur) closes the gap? The balance sheet buys several more years to find out, which is why this remains a speculative option on execution rather than a value situation — the cash cushion prevents near-term ruin but has not, so far, created a floor under the equity.
verification_notes: Share count is now CONFIRMED at 126,139,278 ordinary shares as at 22 September 2026 (Capital Change Notice / ASX Appendix 3G), resolving the prior verification note about the gap between the 124,882,000 shares disclosed at 31 March 2026 and a 2026 substantial-holder notice referencing 126,139,278. RSUs outstanding are confirmed at 8,712,795 following the 2,146,013-unit issuance on 22 September 2026 at a grant price of NZ$1.5720.

Current share price could NOT be pinned to a single precise figure: sources checked on 24-25 September 2026 showed a range from roughly NZ$1.13 (52-week-low reference) to NZ$1.33 (Forsyth Barr NZX quote, 25 September) to AUD$1.215-1.22 (ASX foreign-exempt quote, 24 September) to an isolated outlier of NZ$0.85 that could not be corroborated and is likely a stale or erroneous scrape. The Forsyth Barr NZX quote (NZ$1.33) is used as the primary reference in this analysis as the most directly relevant to the SKO.NZ listing, but all figures should be treated as approximate and refreshed against a live quote before use in any valuation model.

The brief's figure of 'NZ$14-16m of cash' understates Serko's liquidity: NZ$14.146m is cash at bank only; total cash and short-term deposits at 31 March 2026 were NZ$54.1m (NZ$14.146m cash plus NZ$40.0m term deposits), down from NZ$61.4m at March 2025 and NZ$82.0m at September 2024. The going-concern note and all management commentary use the NZ$54.1m figure. No more recent (post-31 March 2026) cash balance has been publicly disclosed as at 26 September 2026 — the Q1 FY2027 update did not include a balance sheet.

Management guidance toward 'cash-flow breakeven / positive free cash flow' could NOT be verified as a formal FY2027 target, and remains unresolved as at September 2026. Neither the FY2026 annual report nor the Q1 FY2027 update contains free cash flow guidance. Secondary reporting of the FY2026 earnings call is internally contradictory (CFO quoted as expecting positive FCF at the guidance midpoint, alongside other commentary citing an expected cash outflow). FY2026 actual free cash flow was negative NZ$4.4m, worse than FY2025's negative NZ$1.9m. Treat FY2027 breakeven as an unconfirmed aspiration.

GetThere migration progress could NOT be verified. Serko has not publicly disclosed a count of GetThere customers migrated to Zeno, an attrition rate, or a revenue-retention figure against what was underwritten at acquisition. The only concrete disclosures are FY2026 revenue of NZ$16.1m, a management expectation of modest DECLINE in FY2027, and H1 FY2026 commentary that 'expected customer exits occurred more slowly' and 'new sales [were] below target'.

Renewal of the Booking.com agreement beyond its 31 March 2029 expiry has NOT been disclosed. No public information was found as at September 2026 regarding renewal discussions, revised terms, or any change to the tiering schedule.

Serko's claim that GetThere is 'the second largest independent corporate booking tool in the US market' is footnoted in its own annual report as 'by volume, based on management estimate' and is not independently verified.

Serko reports as a SINGLE operating segment, so product-level profitability (Booking.com for Business vs Zeno vs GetThere) is not disclosed. The revenue-stream percentages in this analysis are derived from the note 4 revenue disaggregation, not from segment reporting, and no margin can be attributed to any individual product.

'Active customers' (301k FY2026, 325k Q1 FY2027) are Booking.com for Business SME accounts within the partner's platform, NOT Serko's own contracted customers. This metric should not be read as Serko customer relationships.

Insider register: co-founder Bob Shaw disclosed 9,444,678 shares (~7.5%) in a 2026 substantial-holder notice; CEO Darrin Grafton is also a substantial shareholder, increased his holding via RSU vesting around 5 June 2026, and sold ~600,000 shares on-market on 18 July 2026 at ~A$2.66 (reported as ~5.3% of his direct holding and his only on-market trade in the prior twelve months). No director dealings were identified between the July 2026 sale and 26 September 2026. Precise current combined founder ownership percentage as at September 2026 could not be confirmed from primary NZX/ASX filings reviewed.

No new trading update, guidance revision, or investor day has been identified between the Q1 FY2027 update (29 July 2026) and this analysis date (26 September 2026); the continued share price decline in that window therefore appears to reflect sentiment/de-rating rather than a specific disclosed adverse event, based on the sources reviewed.
